title: A Small Tweak to a Simple Classroom Birthday Tradition on-motivation/
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. revisits his long-running classroom birthday ritual of asking each student for a 'word of wisdom' in front of the class and recording it. He explains that the practice is meant to support two of the five key beliefs, credibility and belonging, but that he had noticed three problems: students feel put on the spot, the answers are often flippant or not wise, and a norm of joking responses spreads. His fix is to hand the birthday student an index card with a written note and the same question, to be returned at the end of the hour. The resulting answers were noticeably more thoughtful, no student seemed embarrassed, and the credibility and belonging benefits remained. The post is a small example of auditing a classroom tradition for unintended costs and keeping its motivational purpose while changing the delivery.
points: Even beloved classroom traditions deserve an audit, since public put-on-the-spot formats can embarrass students and invite flippant answers.
Replacing the oral question with a handwritten index-card prompt produced more thoughtful responses and removed the awkwardness.
The tradition is tied to explicit motivation beliefs: tracking birthdays signals care (credibility) and collecting everyone's words signals that all belong.
Offensiveness is a particularly costly way to lose credibility, so avoiding accidental embarrassment is a real gain.
quotes: That last part isn’t good because to feel embarrassed on any day isn’t fun — but how about on your birthday? That’s just a bummer. And the result of this, I suspect, is that over the years I’ve unintentionally offended students through this practice — and as I’ve shared before, research suggests that offensiveness is the worst way to undermine one’s credibility.

And finally, a lot of times I think the silly answers I get to the question are the result of being put on the spot and of seeing previous students get out of the awkwardness by giving a silly answer. And so it can become a norm in some classes that the thing to do with words of wisdom is to say something flippant so Stuart lets you move on with your birthday.
As with all things in my class, I’ve learned that this isn’t just nice, fun, or special. It’s also meant to improve student motivation, specifically in two of the five key beliefs:

Wow! What a difference in quality! Questionable wisdom status: improved. And guess how many of these students seemed to feel “put on the spot” or awkward? Zero. Unintentionally embarrassing students: gone.

I’m still getting the credibility boosts (without nearly as much risk of accidental offensiveness), and I’m still getting the belonging boosts (nobody’s birthday gets missed), and I’ve got the makings of one heck of an end-of-year surprise.
